title: Order matters
prompt: For FizzBuzz (multiples of 3 → "Fizz", of 5 → "Buzz", of both → "FizzBuzz"), why must `n % 15 == 0` be checked first?
options: Because `n % 3 == 0` is also true for 15, so checking it first would print "Fizz" and never reach the FizzBuzz case
It doesn't matter — any order works
explanation: if/else chains stop at the FIRST true branch. When conditions overlap, put the most specific one first.

title: Predict the output: chain order
prompt: Predict what each snippet prints. Watch the order of the thresholds, and look closely at the second `if`.
explanation: 95 >= 70 is true, so the first branch runs and the chain stops — the stricter thresholds are never checked. Put `>= 90` first. In the second snippet, the `;` right after `if (x > 10)` IS the if's (empty) body; the `{ ... }` block below is ordinary code that always runs, so `big` prints even though 3 > 10 is false.

title: Ternary syntax
code:
int max = a > b {{1}} a {{2}} b;
String sign = x >= 0 ? {{3}} : "negative";
explanation: condition `?` whenTrue `:` whenFalse. Both branches must produce a value of the same type.

title: Fall-through
prompt:
With `x = 1`, what does this print?
`switch (x) { case 1: System.out.println("one"); case 2: System.out.println("two"); break; default: System.out.println("other"); }`
options: `one` then `two` — case 1 has no break, so it falls through into case 2
explanation: Without `break`, execution continues into the next case's code. The `break` in case 2 stops it before `default`.

title: FizzBuzz (single value)
prompt: Return `"FizzBuzz"` if `n` is divisible by both 3 and 5, `"Fizz"` if only by 3, `"Buzz"` if only by 5, otherwise the number itself as a string (`String.valueOf(n)`).

solution.explanation: Most specific condition first. `return` exits immediately, so no `else` is needed — a very common clean-code style.

hints: The cases overlap — decide which one must be tested first.
Divisible by both 3 and 5 means divisible by 15.
`String.valueOf(n)` converts an int to a String for the fallback case.

title: Drill: sign of a number
prompt: From memory: return `1` if `x` is positive, `-1` if negative, `0` if zero.

solution.explanation: Three mutually exclusive cases, each ending in an early `return`; whatever survives both checks must be zero. Avoid `x / Math.abs(x)` — it divides by zero at 0 and `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is still negative.

hints: There are exactly three cases; handle two explicitly and let the last be the fallback.
`if (x > 0) return 1;` — then the negative case — then `return 0;`.
